summaries.gardner: Stryker has some Rule Breaker traits, including a top position in robotic joint replacement (Mako) and a strong brand among surgeons, but it is a mature, acquisition-driven leader in established markets, and its shares fell about 17% over the past year. It fits better as a Rule Maker than as an emerging-industry Rule Breaker.
summaries.buffett: Stryker has a durable franchise, consistent profits for decades and a long dividend record, which suits Buffett's preference for understandable businesses with lasting advantages. Returns on capital are only moderate (roughly 13% after tax on LTM operating income) because of acquisition goodwill, debt exceeds cash, and at about 30 times trailing GAAP earnings the price leaves little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the switching costs from Mako and surgeon training and the steady demand from an aging population. He would weigh that against acquisition-heavy capital allocation, $14.9B of debt and a price well above a conservative value; it is a quality business at a full price.
summaries.lynch: Stryker is a classic stalwart: a large company growing revenue about 10-11% a year with adjusted EPS growing 10-12%. Its trailing P/E of about 30 and forward P/E of about 18-20 are above its growth rate, so it fails Lynch's PEG test, and it is widely covered rather than overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Stryker fits Fisher well on new product development (Mako 4, Triathlon Gold, Pangea), a strong sales organization and long-term management continuity, with an internal CEO successor named for 2027. Weaker points are only moderate profit margins on a GAAP basis and growth that leans on acquisitions.
summaries.graham: Stryker fails most of Graham's defensive tests on price: it trades at about 36 times its three-year average earnings, and P/E times P/B is about 144, far above 22.5. It passes on size, earnings stability and its dividend record, but it is not a Graham-style bargain.
summaries.thiel: Stryker is not a zero-to-one company: its technology is better but not ten times better than rivals, and it is a long-established incumbent. Its strengths in Thiel's terms are distribution through a huge sales force and a durable position in concentrated markets.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price with operating discipline. Stryker offers about 9-11% revenue growth, a target of at least 150 basis points of operating margin expansion over three years and a share price down about 17% in a year, but it is not tied to a major platform shift like AI.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on earnings momentum and catalysts 18-24 months out. Stryker's estimates have been trimmed after the cyberattack and supply problems, and the stock is near 52-week lows, so momentum is negative, although the supply recovery and the CEO handover in 2027 could act as catalysts.
summaries.smith: Stryker matches Terry Smith's 'good company' criteria in part: high gross margins (64%), a resilient, non-cyclical healthcare business and steady growth. Its return on capital is only moderate because of goodwill, it carries more debt than cash, and its FCF yield of about 3.8% is not cheap, so it is a good company at a fair to full price.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Stryker scores poorly: LTM operating income of about $5.5B against an enterprise value of about $124B gives an earnings yield of about 4.4%, and return on tangible capital is diluted by acquisitions. It would not rank among Greenblatt's top picks.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool fits partly: Stryker is an above-average business with a strong market position and long-tenured, capable management. The reinvestment leg relies heavily on acquisitions such as Inari rather than high-return organic reinvestment, and returns on capital are only moderate.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at deep discounts. Stryker is low risk but not deeply discounted; even after its fall to about $295, a simple DCF at a 12% discount rate gives roughly $150 a share.
summaries.wood: Stryker is a leader in orthopaedic robotics (Mako), which touches ARK's robotics theme, but it is a diversified incumbent medtech company rather than a disruptive innovation platform. Its markets grow mid-to-high single digits, not exponentially.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry. Stryker fits much of that (predictable, durable franchise, $4.3B of 2025 free cash flow), but the price is not clearly discounted to intrinsic value, and its leverage and steady acquisitions add complexity.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model fits only partly: Stryker grows through volume and new products with little price increase (0.4% in 2025), but it does not explicitly pass scale savings to customers the way Costco or Amazon do. It is a long-duration compounder in steady markets.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and technology-driven disruption at an early stage. Stryker is a mature leader in a large market, not an early-stage disruptor, though Mako showed it can ride technology shifts within orthopaedics.
summaries.nash: Under Tom Nash's process Stryker scores about 70 of 100 and fails several instant-kill tests: debt exceeds cash, current revenue growth is below 10%, and GAAP operating margin was 19.5% in 2025. Its DCF value at a 12% discount rate (about $148) is well below the $294.66 price.

momentum.evidence: SYK closed at $294.66 on October 16, 2026, about 17% below a year earlier, after falling 6.4% on July 31 and 8.8% on September 8, 2026, while the broader market rose.

g4.evidence: Kevin Lobo roughly tripled sales over 14 years as CEO, and 77% of shares are held by institutions, but there are no notable celebrity investors or strategic partners.

g6.evidence: Analysts rate it Moderate Buy with average targets around $372-386 against a $295 price, so it is commonly seen as undervalued rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: Stryker makes implants, surgical tools, robots, hospital beds and vascular devices that hospitals buy repeatedly, which a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Stryker has been profitable every year for decades, and revenue grew from $9.9B in 2015 to $25.1B in 2025, falling only in 2020 because of COVID.

integrity.evidence: Management guides conservatively and pays a rising dividend, but repeated acquisitions, the Q2 2026 supply backorders that lasted longer than guided and securities class-action solicitations raise some questions.

b6.evidence: Stryker has made more than 60 acquisitions under Lobo, mostly tuck-ins, but large deals such as Wright Medical and Inari (about $4.96B of acquisition spending in 2025) show an appetite for building out the portfolio.

roic.evidence: LTM operating income of about $5.5B after a 16% tax rate is about 13% of invested capital (equity $24.0B plus net debt $11.5B), a respectable but not exceptional return that relies partly on debt.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $4.28B (operating cash flow $5.04B less $761M capex), above GAAP net earnings of $3.25B and about 81% of adjusted net earnings.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings reached $20.5B at end-2025 and diluted EPS rose from $4.20 (2020) to $8.40 (2025), but the share price only rose about 11% over five years.

safety.evidence: A DCF using 3-year average growth (10.8%) and FCF margin (15.9%) gives about $148 a share at 12% and about $210 at 10%, below the $294.66 price.

fairprice.evidence: At about 19.6x 2026 and 17.6x 2027 consensus adjusted EPS ($15.00 and $16.74), the price is reasonable for a steady 10% grower, but GAAP P/E is about 30x.

mu5.evidence: Stryker sells many hundreds of products across orthopaedics, surgery, neurotech and hospital equipment, with no single customer or product dominating, so there are few ways it could fail outright.

reinvest.evidence: Stryker can keep reinvesting in R&D ($1.62B in 2025), Mako applications and acquisitions, but returns on those acquisitions are moderate given goodwill of $19.6B.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart: a large, steady company with 10.3% organic growth in 2025 and 8.3-9.3% organic growth guided for 2026.

ly3.evidence: Trailing GAAP P/E of about 30.5 (LTM EPS $9.65) and forward P/E of about 19.6 are both above the roughly 10-12% earnings growth rate.

runway.evidence: An aging population, Mako expansion into shoulder and spine, peripheral vascular through Inari, and international markets (24% of 2025 sales) support many years of growth.

ly7.evidence: Insiders sold about $118.2M of stock over 90 days in mid-2026, and diluted shares rose from 380.3M in 2020 to 386.5M in 2025 with no regular buybacks.

ly8.evidence: Stryker is covered by about 25-27 analysts and is a large S&P 500 company, not overlooked.

fi2.evidence: Management keeps launching new products such as Mako 4 (hip, spine, shoulder), Mako RPS, Triathlon Gold, the Incompass ankle, Pangea plates and the Vocera Sync badge.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $1.62B in 2025 (6.5% of sales) delivered the Mako platform, now installed more than 3,000 times and used in over two-thirds of Stryker's US knees.

fi4.evidence: Stryker is known for a large, aggressive, well-trained sales force, and SG&A of $8.65B (34% of sales) reflects that investment in selling.

longterm.evidence: Stryker invested in Mako for years after buying it in 2013 and keeps funding R&D and acquisitions, accepting near-term margin and impairment costs.

gr1.evidence: Stryker had $25.1B of 2025 sales and a market value of about $113B.

ni10.evidence: Stryker was profitable in each of the last ten years, with GAAP net earnings of $1.99B to $3.25B in each year from 2021 to 2025 and positive in earlier years.

gr4.evidence: Stryker has paid a dividend every year for more than 20 years and raised it again in 2026 to $0.88 a quarter.

th1.evidence: Mako is a leading orthopaedic robot, but rivals such as Zimmer Biomet ROSA and Smith+Nephew CORI offer comparable capabilities, so it is not ten times better.
